title: It's Finished
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: In this personal, reflective post, Dave Stuart Jr. announces that he has completed the manuscript for The Will to Learn, his book on student motivation, after what he describes as a long and painful writing process. He frames the moment through the Greek word tetelestai, "it is finished," the word Jesus speaks from the cross, noting its connotation of both completed action and an ongoing state of rest. Stuart draws a direct parallel between finishing a manuscript and the experience of teaching: time forces educators to finish units, lessons, and school years even when there is always more they wished they could have included. He frames this forced completion not as failure but as an honest feature of creative and pedagogical work, since growth in students and the passage of time are, in his words, tyrants, benevolent or not. The piece closes with a promise to return to more regular blogging now that the manuscript is behind him.
points: Stuart uses the Greek word tetelestai ("it is finished") to reframe completing difficult creative work as both an ending and a settled state, not merely a stopping point.
He explicitly analogizes finishing a book manuscript to finishing a school year or unit: both involve leaving good ideas on the cutting-room floor because time forces closure.
The essay models a teacher publicly naming the emotional cost of long-term creative and professional projects rather than only their triumphant completion.
Stuart frames time and student growth as tyrants, benevolent or not, arguing that educators should expect incompleteness as normal, not a personal failure.
quotes: I just put the final touches on the final draft of the final manuscript of a book I've been working on for what seems like eighty years. It's the one I've mentioned a time or two of late — the one on student motivation.

There's this old Arthur Schopenhauer line where he says that there are two kinds of writers: those who write to write and those who write because they have something to say. I hope to goodness I'm the latter.
I did some research just now on that saying. In the original manuscripts, the word is just the single Greek word tetelestai. It connotes past action and current state.

And it reminds me, quite a bit, of how teaching works, too. Time forces us to "finish" work that, as artists and lovers and creators, we likely never otherwise would. There are always bits that we had hoped would be incorporated into our classes and curricula that don't quite make it to fruition.
And so, not with the authority of Jesus but instead with the tired satisfaction of an imperfect artist, I say, "It's done. Finished. Tetelestai.
